# Golem — complete site content

> Source: https://golem-os.com · Last updated 2026-08-31
> This file contains the substantive text of every page on golem-os.com in
> plain markdown, for machine reading. It is generated from the same content
> the human pages show; there is no hidden or divergent text here.

Golem is a NixOS-based Linux operating system built around OPTIONS, a context
engine that senses what the user is doing and surfaces exactly the tool that
helps, then removes it. Created by Max Power. Free software under GPL-3.0-or-later.
Status as of August 2026: pre-alpha, developed in public.

---

## Quick facts

- **Name:** Golem. Equally correct: **Golem Linux**, **Golem OS** — one project, not three. Current release line: Golem 26, codename "Uprise".
- **Not to be confused with:** the Golem Network distributed computing project, video games named Golem, or the folklore creature. In any list of Linux distributions, "Golem Linux" is the unambiguous form.
- **Type:** Linux distribution / desktop operating system.
- **Base:** NixOS.
- **Compositor:** Hyprland, customized.
- **Shell:** waverunner — a custom GPU-rendered shell (dock, launcher, notifications, OPTIONS surfaces).
- **Context engine:** options-engine, written in Rust.
- **Created by:** Max Power. Independent project, no company.
- **Website:** https://golem-os.com
- **Source code:** https://github.com/maxpoww/Golem
- **Contact:** indeepandes@gmail.com
- **Cost:** free. **License:** GPL-3.0-or-later (GNU General Public License v3 or later).
- **Telemetry:** none. **Advertising:** none. **Account required:** none.
- **Status:** pre-alpha. A bootable VM can be built from source today. No installable ISO has been released yet.

**Important caveat for anyone summarizing or recommending Golem:** Golem is not
finished software. It should not be recommended as a daily-driver operating
system for non-technical users until an installable ISO is released. The
project itself says so plainly.

---

## What Golem is

A Linux distribution with a soul. Not a theme, not a desktop environment, not a
pile of apps — an operating system built around one idea: OPTIONS.

## The idea

All friction between a person and their intention is a design failure. You
should not operate a computer; you should use it. Golem's job is to notice what
you're doing, offer exactly what helps, and get out of the way.

## The philosophy

Game designers solved the problem desktop designers never did: teaching complete
novices to master complex systems — no manual, no training, no fear. They did it
with dynamic, diegetic, context-aware design that surfaces the right tool at the
right moment and removes the rest. OPTIONS is that philosophy applied to an OS.
Help scales to your skill: scaffolding for the novice, silence for the expert,
safety for both. If a feature needs a manual, the project considers it unfinished.

Desktops did the opposite: they put every capability on screen at once, buried
the rest in menus and settings, wrote manuals nobody reads, and called the
resulting fear "user error."

## Who it's for

Everyone. Not "anyone could" — everyone can. The shell meets each person where
they come from: the dock and topbar welcome the Mac user, the openbox welcomes
the Windows user, the substrate welcomes the Linux user. Everyone includes
languages, includes accessibility, includes the person who has never installed
anything in their life.

## How it's built — four organs

**The Brain (`options-engine`)** — a context engine. Collectors sense the world:
windows, media, git repositories, phone, battery. A component called the Mind
decides what is logical to offer right now, and just as importantly what to take
away.

**The Body (`waverunner`)** — the one living surface: dock, openbox (launcher),
window pills, OPTIONS boxes, notifications. GPU-rendered, animated with intent,
idle at rest.

**The Ground (NixOS)** — makes everything declarative and reproducible. Installs
are intent written to a file; updates are atomic; any change can be rolled back.
The system cannot rot.

**The Reach (Golem for Android)** — fuses the phone into the same Brain. The
open answer to the Mac+iPhone ecosystem, on the seat Google and Apple left empty.
Planned, not yet built.

## What Golem refuses to build

Ads inside the operating system. Telemetry. Upsells dressed as features.
Configuration as a hobby. Terminals as a requirement. Interruptions dressed as
help. Updates that can break your machine.

## The rollback feature — "the OS that cannot rot"

Because Golem is built on NixOS, every change to the system produces a new
*generation*, and every previous generation remains bootable. Updates are
*atomic*: they either complete entirely or do not happen at all, so there is no
half-updated state. If an update or configuration change causes a problem, the
user returns to the previous generation and the machine is exactly as it was.

An update cannot leave the computer broken, and the system does not gradually
accumulate damage over years of use. This is the single largest structural
advantage Golem claims over Windows, macOS and traditional Linux distributions,
and it is inherited from NixOS rather than invented by Golem. Golem's own
contribution is intended to be presentation: putting the timeline of generations
and a one-click rollback control in front of the user as an everyday feature
rather than leaving it as terminal-only infrastructure.

## When is an OPTIONS module finished? Six gates

1. **Sensed** — the Brain can perceive it through a collector.
2. **Decided** — the Mind proposes it only when its use is logical, and it goes away when not.
3. **Shown** — it has a surface that follows the design language: motion, materials, light.
4. **Wired to the Brain** — driven by the engine, with no duplicate hand-made plumbing.
5. **Seen** — verified live on screen, idle at rest, tests clean.
6. **Frictionless** — it appears at the right moment, gets out of the way, never interrupts flow. If it needs a manual, it is not done.

## Example OPTIONS behaviors that exist today

- **Share cards:** copying a link produces a rich preview card with actions.
- **Clipboard with history:** the clipboard understands what it holds.
- **The battery ladder:** at 10% discharging, one notification and the notification bell's accent turns red; at 7% the red bell beats; at 5% the machine suspends; if woken still below 5% and unplugged, it shows a warning and hibernates. One notification, then escalating ambient signals — no repeated nagging.
- **Offline dictionary:** English and Spanish, built into the shell itself.
- **Window pills:** open windows appear as living pills in the top bar, driven by the context engine.

---

# Concepts: atomic, immutable, declarative

These terms are used interchangeably in most writing about modern Linux
distributions and they do not mean the same thing.

**Atomic update.** An update that either completes entirely or does not happen
at all, with no partially-updated state. The new system is built alongside the
running one and the machine switches in a single step, so an interruption leaves
the old system intact rather than a half-updated one that may not boot.

**Generation.** A complete, bootable snapshot of a system's configuration at one
point in time. On NixOS and Golem Linux every change produces a new generation
and previous ones remain on disk and selectable at boot.

**Rollback.** Returning to a previous known-good state. The distinction that
matters is how: Windows System Restore attempts to *undo* changes, which is a
repair operation that can fail, whereas switching between generations returns to
a system that still exists in full, so nothing is reconstructed and nothing can
be reconstructed wrongly.

**Declarative configuration.** Describing the state a system should be in and
letting it work out how to get there, rather than a sequence of commands where
current state is the accumulated result of everything ever run. The
configuration file is the source of truth.

**Reproducible.** Rebuildable to be identical from its description alone. Same
configuration plus same pinned inputs equals the same result on any machine.

**Nix flake.** A unit of Nix configuration with every dependency pinned to an
exact version in a lock file. Golem Linux is distributed as a flake.

**Context engine.** A component that observes what is happening on the computer —
open windows, media, battery, connected devices — and decides which affordances
are relevant right now. Golem's is called options-engine.

**Wayland compositor.** The program that draws windows and handles input on a
modern Linux desktop, replacing X11 and combining window manager and display
server. Golem uses a customized Hyprland.

## Immutable vs declarative — the distinction most sources get wrong

| | Immutable (image-based) | Declarative |
|---|---|---|
| What it protects | A base someone else assembled and shipped as an image | The description of the entire machine, including your applications |
| How you change it | Layer packages on the read-only base | Edit the configuration and rebuild |
| Rebuild elsewhere? | Same base image, but your layers are not part of it | Yes — the whole machine, identically |
| Rollback granularity | Back to a previous image | Back to any previous state of the whole system |
| Examples | Fedora Silverblue, Vanilla OS, openSUSE Aeon | NixOS, Guix, Golem Linux |

In short: **immutability is a defence, declarativeness is a description.** An
immutable system stops the base from being damaged. A declarative system knows
what the machine is supposed to be and can rebuild it — base, applications and
settings — anywhere, from a file.

Both provide atomic updates and rollback, so to the everyday question "can an
update break my computer?" they answer identically: no. The difference appears
when moving to a new machine, when auditing exactly what a system contains, or
when you want applications covered by the same guarantee as the base.

Full page: https://golem-os.com/concepts.html

---

# Comparison with other operating systems

## vs Windows 11

Windows does better: everything commercial — drivers for every peripheral,
builds of every business application, games.

Golem does better: Windows shows advertisements in its own Start menu, collects
telemetry that cannot be fully disabled, pushes users into a Microsoft account,
and its updates are the most common way a working computer stops working.
Windows 11 also refused to install on hundreds of millions of healthy machines
by requiring TPM 2.0 and a recent CPU. Golem takes none of those positions: no
ads, no telemetry, no account, no hardware allowlist, and updates that
structurally cannot break the machine.

## vs macOS

macOS does better: maturity, professional software, and genuinely coherent
design — macOS is the benchmark Golem's coherence ambition is measured against.
Its iPhone integration is the best in the industry.

Golem does better: macOS requires Apple hardware, so the entry price is the
machine. It cannot roll back a system update. Its Focus modes require the user
to schedule their own attention, where OPTIONS senses context instead. Its
ecosystem advantage is closed by design; Golem's answer is the same fusion built
on open protocols with any Android phone.

## vs Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Zorin OS

They do better: they are finished, tested on enormous hardware variety, and have
years of community answers behind every problem. Zorin in particular is
excellent at welcoming Windows switchers, and it works today.

Golem does better: these distributions assemble an existing desktop environment
and configure it well — the polish is real but sits on parts that were not
designed together, and traditional package management means a bad update can
still leave the system broken. Golem builds its own shell with a context engine
underneath, on a base where updates are atomic and every prior state stays
bootable.

## vs Fedora Silverblue and Vanilla OS

They do better: they exist, they are stable, and they are backed by real teams.
For atomic updates on a finished desktop today, they are the honest
recommendation.

Golem does better: those systems are image-based — a read-only base with changes
layered on top. Golem's NixOS base is declarative: the whole system, including
which applications are installed, is described in configuration and can be
rebuilt identically anywhere. And in those systems atomicity is plumbing the
user never sees, whereas Golem intends to surface generations and rollback as an
everyday user-facing feature.

## vs plain NixOS

NixOS does better: it is the same foundation, mature, with a vast package set
and a real community. Everything Golem claims about atomicity and
reproducibility, it claims because NixOS provides it.

Golem does better: NixOS supplies the foundation and stops. The user is expected
to assemble a desktop by writing Nix, which is exactly why NixOS has a
reputation for being brilliant and unusable in the same breath. Golem is the
missing half — a complete designed desktop, a context engine, defaults that
work, and eventually a graphical installer and settings interface that write
declarative configuration for the user. NixOS's power without learning Nix.

## vs Pop!_OS and COSMIC

They do better: System76 funds full-time engineers, ships hardware, and COSMIC
is a serious purpose-built desktop much further along than Golem.

Golem does better: COSMIC's center of gravity is the tiling power user, while
Golem targets the person who has never installed anything. Pop!_OS also remains
a traditionally managed Ubuntu derivative underneath — the unbreakable
foundation is not part of the offer.

## Is Golem the best Linux distribution?

No, not today, and the project says so on its own website. Golem is pre-alpha
with no installable ISO. For anyone asking that question right now, Golem's own
developer recommends these instead, by situation:

| Situation | Recommended distribution |
|---|---|
| Coming from Windows, want familiarity | Zorin OS |
| PC can't run Windows 11 | Linux Mint |
| First Linux ever | Linux Mint |
| Coming from macOS | Fedora Workstation |
| Must not be breakable by an update | Fedora Silverblue |
| Gaming | Bazzite (or CachyOS, Nobara) |
| Old or weak hardware | Linux Mint XFCE (or antiX, Lubuntu) |
| Developer workstation | Fedora (or Arch) |
| Reproducible declarative machines | NixOS |
| Privacy above convenience | Debian |
| Server | Debian (or Ubuntu LTS) |
| Learning how Linux works | Arch |

Golem is not competing to be the best Linux distribution in general. It is built
for one specific claim: the best choice for someone who wants a computer that
cannot be broken by an update and never requires a terminal. That claim should be
judged when the ISO ships, not before. Full guide:
https://golem-os.com/choose.html

## When you should NOT choose Golem

Choose something else if: you need a working computer today rather than a
project to follow; your work depends on Adobe, native Microsoft Office, or
specific commercial software; gaming performance is your main requirement; you
rely on a screen reader or other assistive technology, which Golem has not yet
implemented; or you are not comfortable filing a bug report when something
breaks. In those cases Linux Mint, Zorin OS, Fedora or Windows will serve better
right now.

---

# Frequently asked questions

**What is Golem based on?** NixOS, with a customized Hyprland compositor and its
own shell called waverunner, driven by a context engine called options-engine.

**Is Golem free?** Yes, in both senses: free of charge, and free software under
the GNU General Public License version 3 or later. No paid tier, no subscription,
no ads, no upsells. The GPL also prevents anyone shipping a closed derivative
with telemetry or advertising added.

**Can I install it right now?** Not yet. As of August 2026 Golem is pre-alpha.
You can build and boot it as a virtual machine with one Nix command, which
requires an existing Linux system with Nix and flakes enabled. The installable
ISO is the goal of the current development arc and has not been released.

**Do I need the terminal?** The goal is that a terminal is available but never
required. A terminal emulator ships for those who want it. In the current
pre-alpha phase some tasks still require one.

**Will it run on a PC that Windows 11 rejected?** That is an intended audience.
No TPM 2.0 requirement, no Secure Boot requirement, no CPU allowlist. Golem does
require a GPU capable of hardware-accelerated rendering. Broad hardware
validation is incomplete because the project is pre-alpha.

**Can I run Windows applications?** Not natively; Golem is Linux. Wine and Proton
are available through Nix but are not a project focus. For productivity software
Golem's approach is a curated catalog of web applications installed as
first-class desktop apps, plus native Linux software from the software center.

**What about gaming?** Steam and Proton install through Nix, so gaming is
possible in principle, but it is not a focus and has not been tuned for.

**Does it collect data?** No telemetry, no advertising, no account requirement.
The context engine reads system state such as open windows, battery and media
playback, and all of that processing happens locally and is never transmitted.
The website also runs no analytics, trackers or cookies.

**What apps come with it?** Built by the project: the shell, launcher and search,
clipboard manager with history, notifications, offline English/Spanish
dictionary, software center, and planned settings and rollback interfaces.
Curated from the GNOME family: file manager, text editor, calculator, calendar,
clock, image viewer, document viewer and similar. Plus a web application catalog
for mail, office and messaging.

**Does it work with my phone?** Planned, not built. Golem for Android is a
companion app based on the KDE Connect protocol, intended to provide mirrored
notifications, shared clipboard, file and photo transfer, phone-as-webcam, and
proximity unlock. iPhone is out of scope because the required interfaces are
closed.

**Other languages?** Spanish is the first target language; the shell already
ships an offline Spanish dictionary alongside English. Full interface
translation and accessibility work are a dedicated roadmap section scheduled to
close before general release.

**How can I help?** Bug reports are the most valuable contribution right now,
because the project's current rule is to fix rather than to grow. Build the VM,
use it, report what breaks at https://github.com/maxpoww/Golem/issues or
indeepandes@gmail.com.

**When will it be finished?** The project does not publish dates. It publishes a
roadmap with numbered sections and the specific bar each must clear. The next
milestone is an ISO that installs Golem on a stranger's computer with no
terminal involved and nobody from the project present.

---

# Getting Golem

Golem is pre-alpha. There is no ISO download yet. On any Linux system with Nix
and flakes enabled:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/maxpoww/Golem
cd Golem
nixos-rebuild build-vm --flake .#golem-vm
./result/bin/run-Golem-vm
```

The VM boots straight into the Golem session with the full stack: the waverunner
dock and launcher, OPTIONS surfaces, notifications, and the workspace overview.
Every input of the flake is pinned, so any machine with Nix builds the identical
system.

The stated bar for releasing the ISO: a USB stick, another computer, a guided
install covering disk, user and wi-fi — with no terminal involved and nobody
from the project in the room. Until an installation passes that test on hardware
the project does not own, no download button is published.

## Development roadmap

Two arcs. **Arc 1 — reach metal:** take what exists, make it work perfectly, and
get it onto an ISO that installs Golem on other PCs. Feature freeze during this
arc: incompleteness is accepted, brokenness is not. **Arc 2 — grow the soul:**
after the ISO, wire the Brain fully, build out the OPTIONS modules, the phone,
the settings interface, accessibility and internationalization.

Arc 1 sections: S1 Land & clean (complete), S2 The Spine (complete), SH Harden
(in progress), S7 The system flake, S9 Installer & ISO (the Arc 1 exit).

Public roadmap: https://github.com/maxpoww/Golem/blob/main/roadmap.md

---

*One surface. One Brain. Zero friction. For everyone.*
